name: PIQP
workload: Convex QP solve time on the Maros-Meszaros test set (138 problems; 76-problem sparse subset), shifted geometric mean of runtime over four accuracy settings, run through the qpsolvers Python wrappers.
claimed_speedup: Independent qpbenchmark v2.3.0, Maros-Meszaros (138 problems), runtime shifted geometric mean with PIQP = 1.0: OSQP 12.7 (default), 16.1 (high accuracy), 52.8 (low), 51.9 (mid); sparse subset (76 problems): OSQP 9.5 / 17.4 / 30.0 / 56.0. Success rate at default settings 95.7% for PIQP vs 43.5% for OSQP. First-party piqp_benchmarks (shifted geometric means, PIQP = 1.0): OSQP 7.55 at low accuracy and 42.66 at high accuracy.
hardware: qpbenchmark run: Intel Core i7-6500U @ 2.50GHz (4 logical CPUs). First-party piqp_benchmarks: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3990X 64-core @ 4.3GHz.
tradeoffs: Convex QPs only. Header-only C++14 built on Eigen, with dense, sparse and multistage backends; C/C++, Python, Matlab/Octave and R interfaces. Proximal interior-point method, so it needs sparse/dense LDL factorizations per iteration.
caveats: Category fit is loose: this is a QP optimization solver, not a sparse linear-system solver, and OSQP is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc baseline list. The qpbenchmark was run through prebuilt Python wheels (solver versions piqp 0.4.1, osqp 0.6.7.post0, qpsolvers 4.3.3), so no compiler or flags apply. Its own known-limitations list includes CPU thermal throttling (issue 88). Failed solves are counted at the 1000 s time limit, which inflates the ratios of solvers that fail often. Results are shifted geometric means on one test set; ProxQP's own benchmark (different problem classes) shows ProxQP ahead of OSQP instead, so rankings depend on the suite.
found_via: PyPI JSON https://pypi.org/pypi/piqp/json (after PyPI name scan for qpsolvers / qpsolvers_benchmark), then the qpsolvers Maros-Meszaros results page and https://github.com/PREDICT-EPFL/piqp_benchmarks

name: QPALM
workload: Convex QP solve time on the Maros-Meszaros test set (138 problems; 76-problem sparse subset), shifted geometric mean of runtime over four accuracy settings, run through the qpsolvers Python wrappers.
claimed_speedup: Independent qpbenchmark v2.3.0, Maros-Meszaros (138 problems), runtime shifted geometric mean (best solver = 1.0, which is PIQP): QPALM 3.6 vs OSQP 12.7 (default), 4.8 vs 16.1 (high accuracy), 3.4 vs 52.8 (low), 2.2 vs 51.9 (mid). Sparse subset (76 problems): QPALM 3.2 vs OSQP 9.5 (default), 4.3 vs 17.4, 3.1 vs 30.0, 1.8 vs 56.0. Success rate at default settings 55.8% vs 43.5% for OSQP.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6500U @ 2.50GHz (4 logical CPUs), run by a third party (qpsolvers maintainer)
tradeoffs: Proximal augmented-Lagrangian QP solver that also handles nonconvex QPs; C core with C++, Python, Julia, Matlab and Fortran interfaces; LGPL copyleft.
caveats: Category fit is loose: QP optimization solver, not a linear-system solver; OSQP is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc list. Result is from prebuilt Python wheels (qpalm 1.2.3, osqp 0.6.7.post0), so no compiler or flags; known limitation of the suite includes CPU thermal throttling. QPALM is itself about 2-5x slower than PIQP in the same table. The QPALM repo page opened only gave paper references, no numbers of its own. Failed solves are counted at the 1000 s time limit.
found_via: PyPI name scan (qpsolvers, qpsolvers_benchmark) -> qpsolvers Maros-Meszaros qpbenchmark results page; repo page opened separately

name: ProxQP (ProxSuite)
baseline: OSQP (also compared against Gurobi, MOSEK, qpOASES, quadprog)
workload: Randomly generated dense and sparse (about 15% density) convex QPs and the hard Maros-Meszaros problems, shifted geometric mean of solve time at high accuracy (eps 1e-9) and low accuracy (1e-3).
claimed_speedup: First-party proxqp_benchmark, shifted geometric means with PROXQP = 1.0, high accuracy: dense random QPs OSQP 18.2, qpOASES 282.6, quadprog 20.4; sparse (~15%) random QPs OSQP 3.5, qpOASES 260.6, quadprog 19.3; Maros-Meszaros OSQP 14.2, qpOASES 4.5, Gurobi 114.2 (low accuracy 1e-3: OSQP 108.5, qpOASES 17.1).
stars_or_usage: 594 stars; vcpkg port proxsuite; PyPI proxsuite
tradeoffs: Dense and sparse backends, Eigen-based, vectorized and allocation-free updates, Python bindings; targets robotics (MPC) use. Convex QPs.
caveats: First-party benchmark (tier C): the proxqp_benchmark scripts are public and the CPU is named, but no compiler, flags or solver versions are given. The benchmark covers the dense ProxQP backend only. The independent qpbenchmark (Maros-Meszaros, i7-6500U) is mixed: runtime shifted geometric mean 53.3 for ProxQP vs 12.7 for OSQP at default settings (ProxQP slower), but 5.9 vs 16.1 at high accuracy, 36.0 vs 52.8 at low and 19.2 vs 51.9 at mid (ProxQP faster); ProxQP success rate 73.2% vs OSQP 43.5% at default. Category fit is loose (QP optimization, not linear-system solving) and OSQP is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc list.
found_via: vcpkg port https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/vcpkg/master/ports/proxsuite/vcpkg.json and PyPI https://pypi.org/pypi/proxsuite/json; benchmark from the repo README link

name: Spectra
workload: Median elapsed time to compute a few eigenpairs of symmetric and general test matrices with Spectra versus ARPACK (Fortran wrapper), using the benchmark/ program in the repo.
claimed_speedup: Project performance page (spectralib.org/performance.html) is reported by a search-result excerpt to say the symmetric eigen solver is uniformly faster than ARPACK in all tested cases and the general solver is about the same as ARPACK. No numbers were obtained: that site is blocked from this container and the GitHub README gives none.
compiler_and_flags: benchmark/Makefile: g++ -Wall -O2 for the C++/Spectra side, gfortran -O3 for the ARPACK wrapper, linked with -larpack -llapack -lblas
stars_or_usage: 866 stars; vcpkg port spectra and Conan recipe spectra exist
tradeoffs: Header-only on top of Eigen; matrix-free operators and Eigen sparse matrices; implicitly restarted Arnoldi/Lanczos. Not an ARPACK clone and does not use ARPACK code.
caveats: Numbers could not be opened in this session, so the claim is qualitative; the excerpt also named Solus 4.2, Clang 11.1.0, OpenBLAS 0.3.15 single-threaded, Spectra v1.0.0 and ARPACK-NG 3.7.0, which a verifier should confirm on the page. The benchmark program in the repo builds dense MatrixXd test matrices, so it says little about sparse performance. Results depend on which BLAS ARPACK is linked against. ARPACK is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc baseline list (PETSc users reach it through SLEPc).
found_via: vcpkg port https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/vcpkg/master/ports/spectra/vcpkg.json and Conan recipe probe (conan-center-index/recipes/spectra); repo benchmark directory opened

name: ALP/GraphBLAS (nonblocking backend)
workload: PageRank, conjugate gradient and sparse DNN inference on ten sparse matrices (per a search-result excerpt of the paper), ALP/GraphBLAS nonblocking execution compared with Eigen and SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS.
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed paper (Mastoras, Anagnostidis, Yzelman, ACM TACO 20(1), 2022, doi 10.1145/3561652) reports the nonblocking ALP/GraphBLAS faster than both Eigen and SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS on PageRank, CG and sparse DNN inference. Figures are not verified here: see caveats.
stars_or_usage: 33 stars; PyPI package alp-graphblas (pyalp bindings, backends pyalp_ref, pyalp_omp, pyalp_nonblocking)
tradeoffs: Header-based C++11 framework needing OpenMP, libnuma, pthreads and CMake; run-time fusion of linear-algebra primitives (nonblocking mode) and shared/distributed-memory backends. GraphBLAS-style API rather than an Eigen- or PETSc-style API.
caveats: I could not open the paper (dl.acm.org, arxiv.org and researchgate.net are blocked from this container) and the ALP README contains no numbers. The only figures I saw were in a search-result excerpt of the abstract: up to 12.2x over Eigen and 16.1x over SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS, and up to 5.13x over ALP's own blocking mode. A verifier must open the paper to confirm the numbers, matrices, CPU, compiler and flags. Gains are specific to algorithms that chain GraphBLAS primitives and benefit from fusion, so single-kernel speedups are likely smaller.
found_via: PyPI name scan: https://pypi.org/pypi/alp-graphblas/json -> GitHub repo; WebSearch 'ALP GraphBLAS nonblocking speedup SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS LAGraph benchmark Algebraic Programming'

name: PanguLU
workload: Distributed sparse LU factorization and solve of sparse test matrices on CPU+GPU clusters (up to 128 NVIDIA A100 and 128 AMD MI50 GPUs, per a search-result excerpt of the SC'23 paper abstract).
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed paper (PanguLU, SC '23) reports speedups over SuperLU_DIST on 128-GPU heterogeneous platforms. Exact figures are not verified here: see caveats.
tradeoffs: Written in C with MPI, OpenMP and CUDA; regular 2D block-cyclic layout with sparse blocks and synchronisation-free communication; optional METIS and MC64 reordering; real and complex, single and double precision. AGPL-3.0 copyleft. Tested with MPICH 4.3.0, CUDA 12.9, OpenBLAS 0.3.26 per README.
caveats: I could not open the paper (dl.acm.org, arxiv.org and researchgate.net are blocked here) and the GitHub README has no performance numbers. The figures I saw were in a search-result excerpt: up to 11.70x (128 A100) and 17.97x (128 MI50) over SuperLU_DIST, with scaling of 47.51x and 74.84x over one GPU. A verifier must confirm these, the SuperLU_DIST version, matrices, compiler and flags. Distributed heterogeneous-system result, so single-node CPU users may see very different ratios. SuperLU_DIST is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc list (PETSc can call it). Last commit is 14 months before the run date.
found_via: WebSearch 'PanguLU sparse direct solver faster than SuperLU_DIST github speedup'; repo opened via the SuperScientificSoftwareLaboratory organisation page and raw README

name: sparse_dot_topn
baseline: SciPy sparse CSR matrix multiplication (scipy.sparse A.dot(B), SciPy 1.12.0)
workload: Sparse matrix product A.dot(B) of two TF-IDF CSR matrices of shape (20,000 x 193,190) by (193,190 x 20,000) built from SEC EDGAR company names, with and without keeping only the top-n values per row; 30 repeats.
claimed_speedup: Apple M2 Pro, 8 threads: plain sp_matmul 5.1x faster than SciPy (0.032 s vs 0.165 s min time); sp_matmul_topn with top_n=10 and 8 threads 6.9x faster (0.024 s). Intel i9 2.3 GHz 8-core, 8 threads: sp_matmul 3.4x. Single-thread plain product about 1.0x on M2 Pro.
hardware: Apple MacBook Pro M2 Pro (32GB RAM); MacBook Pro 2.3 GHz 8-core Intel Core i9 (16GB RAM)
tradeoffs: Python package with a C++17 extension (OpenMP vendored); uses a max-heap to keep memory low when only the top-n entries per row are needed. Result type and API differ from plain SciPy products. Not a general SpGEMM replacement.
caveats: First-party benchmark (tier C): bench code is public and hardware is named but compiler and flags are not. SciPy's sparse matmul is single-threaded, so almost all of the speedup comes from multithreading; single-thread plain product is about 1.0x. The top-n variant is slower than SciPy for large n (for example 6.2x slower at top_n=1000 on one thread on the M2 Pro). SciPy CSR matmul is not SuiteSparse, Eigen or PETSc, so baseline_in_list is false and the category fit is partial.
found_via: PyPI JSON scan of sparse-related package descriptions (https://pypi.org/pypi/sparse-dot-topn/json): line 'up to 6 times faster'

name: spla (JetBrains Research sparse linear algebra)
baseline: LaGraph on SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS (also GraphBLAST and Gunrock as other contenders)
workload: Graph algorithms expressed as generalized sparse linear algebra on SuiteSparse-collection and SNAP/LAW graphs (PageRank named in README), run on NVIDIA, Intel and AMD GPUs including integrated GPUs; speedup relative to LaGraph (SuiteSparse) on CPU.
claimed_speedup: README plots 'relative speedup of GraphBLAST, Gunrock and Spla compared to a LaGraph (SuiteSparse) used a baseline' on a logarithmic scale, and a second plot of Spla alone on integrated Intel HD Graphics 530 and AMD GFX1036 GPUs; the text gives no numeric speedups beyond 'much faster than scipy or networkx' and claims better results than GraphBLAST on large graphs and than Gunrock on PageRank.
compiler_and_flags: Clang with C++17 support; build.py --build-type=Release (no other flags listed)
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04, Intel Core i7-6700 4-core 3.40GHz, 64GB DDR4, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070; Ubuntu 22.04, AMD Ryzen 9 7900X, 128GB DDR4, AMD GFX1036 integrated GPU; also Intel Arc A770 and AMD Radeon Vega Frontier Edition for the scaling plot
tradeoffs: OpenCL-based GPU backend with a C++ API and Python bindings; works on Intel, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. GraphBLAS-like generalized sparse linear algebra, not a solver library.
caveats: Numbers exist only inside plot images on the README, none in text, so the speedup values are unverified from the page I read. The README itself says 'project under heavy development! Not ready for usage.' The comparison is GPU versus a CPU LaGraph baseline whose thread count is not stated. Graph analytics rather than numerical solvers, so category fit is partial.
found_via: PyPI JSON https://pypi.org/pypi/pyspla/json (name scan for sparse libraries) -> GitHub README performance section

name: VBCSR
workload: Variable-block sparse matrix operations (README table of 500 to 20,000 blocks, about 9,000 to 360,000 rows; the repo's report script uses block sizes 16-20), VBCSR versus SciPy, serial run.
claimed_speedup: README table: 4.21x at 500 blocks (0.0049 s vs 0.0209 s), 4.07x at 1,000 blocks, 4.33x at 5,000 blocks, 4.46x at 10,000 blocks, 4.49x at 20,000 blocks (0.1866 s vs 0.8377 s) over SciPy.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ core with pybind11 Python bindings, MPI-distributed variable-block CSR, AVX/AVX2 SIMD, thresholded SpMM; targets localized-orbital Hamiltonians and multi-DOF PDE systems. AGPL-3.0 copyleft. Needs MPI and BLAS/LAPACK.
caveats: First-party table with no CPU, compiler, flags or thread count, and the README table does not say which operation (the page mentions SpMV and SpMM) is timed. The repo also benchmarks against sparse_dot_mkl (MKL) but that result is not in the README I read. SciPy is not SuiteSparse, Eigen or PETSc, so baseline_in_list is false. Very small project (1 star); README clone URL is a placeholder.
found_via: PyPI JSON scan of sparse-related package descriptions (https://pypi.org/pypi/vbcsr/json) with repo URL taken from the sdist's conda recipe

name: ALBUS
baseline: Intel MKL SpMV (oneAPI 2021); also CSR5 and merge-based SpMV
workload: Double-precision CSR SpMV (GFlops) on 40 SuiteSparse/UF matrices (20 regular, 20 irregular) on dual-socket Xeon CPUs, OpenMP plus AVX2.
claimed_speedup: README quotes the FGCS 2021 abstract: on dual-socket Xeon E5-2670 v3, regular matrices average 1.59x / 1.32x / 1.48x (up to 2.53x / 2.22x / 2.31x) over CSR5 / Merge / MKL; irregular matrices average 1.38x / 1.42x / 2.44x (up to 2.33x / 2.24x / 5.37x) over CSR5 / Merge / MKL. README per-matrix table (Xeon Gold 6242 dual socket, GFlops): rma10 ALBUS 94.52 vs CSR5 42.05 vs CVR 65.84; mac_econ_fwd500 68.56 vs 25.33 vs 40.79; webbase-1M 34.14 vs 21.92 vs 22.13; ALBUS loses to CVR on cant, ins2 and pdb1HYS.
compiler_and_flags: icpc -xCORE-AVX2 -qopt-prefetch=3 -fopenmp -O3 for the ALBUS builds (README Makefile); baselines' build flags not stated
hardware: README table: dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6242 (2 x 16 cores); abstract numbers: dual-socket Xeon E5-2670 v3; README also names dual-socket Xeon Silver 4110
stars_or_usage: 17 stars; paper: Bian et al., Future Generation Computer Systems 116 (2021) 371-392
tradeoffs: Research code (main.cpp plus headers, not a packaged library); needs a conversion/preprocessing step into the ALBUS format; AVX2-oriented and built with the Intel compiler; OpenMP and OpenMP+AVX2 variants.
caveats: The MKL and Merge columns of the README table are empty, so the MKL and Merge comparison rests on the paper abstract quoted in the README, which was measured on a different CPU (E5-2670 v3) than the table (Gold 6242). Baseline codes (CSR5, CVR, Merge, MKL) are not in the repo, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from it alone, and conversion/preprocessing cost is not shown. Last commit 2022. Baselines are not SuiteSparse, Eigen or PETSc (MKL is a widely used incumbent; CSR5 and merge-spmv are already catalogued).
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/sparse-matrix-vector-multiplication (not a package registry; found after the registry scans came up thin)

name: sparsam
workload: End-to-end Gauss-Newton/LM optimization of the 2D M3500 pose graph using sparsam's own block-sparse Cholesky with AMD ordering, versus GTSAM 4.2; bundle adjustment on BAL Ladybug versus Ceres 2.2.
claimed_speedup: README: on M3500 sparsam's GN/LM is 1.7-2.1x faster end-to-end than GTSAM 4.2 at final chi-squared parity of 0.009%. Against Ceres 2.2 on BAL Ladybug bundle adjustment sparsam is slower in wall clock (1.74 s vs 0.67 s on ladybug-49, 1.57 s vs 0.48 s on ladybug-73, 9.9 s vs 4.9 s on ladybug-138, 26.5 s vs 24.0 s on ladybug-318) but 552 vs 1091 ms per iteration on ladybug-318.
tradeoffs: SLAM and estimation backend written from scratch in C++20 using only the standard library and Eigen dense fixed-size types; own CSR-of-blocks storage, AMD/RCM ordering and simplicial block Cholesky. Not a general sparse solver API. Benchmarks need GTSAM and Ceres built behind an off-by-default CMake flag.
caveats: Mixed result that the README itself states: Ceres wins wall clock on bundle adjustment, and on fill-heavy 3D pose graphs GTSAM's per-iteration linear algebra is about 3-5x faster than sparsam's simplicial block Cholesky. The M3500 speedup is end to end (including iteration counts and damping strategy), not a like-for-like factorization time. Author-run, single machine, GTSAM/Ceres build flags not stated in the README, and the project is weeks old with 1 star. Category fit is loose (nonlinear least-squares/SLAM backend whose core is sparse Cholesky); baselines are not SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse or PETSc.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/sparse-linear-algebra?l=c%2B%2B (not a package registry)
